title: The Toilet Paper Tariff
trigger_signal: Guardian/HN story on surging toilet-paper prices (Aug 26, 102 pts) + Google Trends 'toilet paper prices' +390% WoW + GDELT tariff-coverage volume +12%, three independent sources corroborating in one week (research note 14 (private)).
thesis: The Canada tariff didn't tax Canadians, it taxed the American buying paper towels, because pulp is an integrated cross-border supply chain with no fast substitute.

sources.claim_it_supports: The 14% tariff rate on Canadian paper products applied to landed cost, and the effective date it took effect (shots 3, 4, 9).
HTS heading 4803 is the correct tariff-schedule classification for tissue-grade paper referenced on screen in shot 9.
Kimberly-Clark's most recent 10-Q language on recovering higher input costs through pricing (shots 11, 12).
Cross-border pulp share (two-thirds of US-bound pulp crosses from Canada) and the $1.10 shelf-price cost-stack breakdown (retailer ~25c, mill ~30c, tree ~5c) in shots 5, 13, 14, 15.
New pulp mill construction cost (~$2B) and build timeline (3-5 years), supporting the 'no fast substitute' claim in shot 7.

shots.script_line: A nine-dollar pack of paper towels went to eleven dollars last month, and nobody at the store can tell you why...
shots.on_screen: Shelf price tag, $8.99 crossed out, $10.99 sticker. Slow push-in.

tool_params.prompt: grocery store shelf price tag, $8.99 crossed out with a red sticker reading $10.99, paper towel packs in soft background blur, house style board

shots.script_line: ...because the honest answer involves three governments, a pulp mill in Quebec, and a tariff schedule nobody reads past the headline.
shots.on_screen: The Ledger opens; three line items stamp in: '3 governments · 1 pulp mill · 1 tariff schedule'.

shots.script_line: Here's the number: the new tariff on Canadian paper products sits at 14 percent. Not 14 percent on the shelf price -- 14 percent on the landed cost...
shots.on_screen: Animated map: Quebec mill -> border -> US converter -> retailer; '14%' stamp lands at the border.

shots.script_line: ...the tariff taxes the input, and then everyone downstream marks up their own margin on the more expensive input. That's how 14 percent becomes 20-plus at the register.
shots.on_screen: Cost-stack bar builds: pulp -> +tariff -> converter markup -> retail markup. Numbers count up.

shots.script_line: Two-thirds of the pulp that becomes American toilet paper crosses the Canadian border first...

search_terms: logging truck snowy road public domain

shots.script_line: ...the supply chain was integrated on purpose, decades ago, back when nobody planned for a trade war over lumber and paper.
shots.on_screen: Slow H3 motion: pulp bales moving on a conveyor, no people in frame.

tool_params.prompt: pulp bales moving on an industrial conveyor belt, interior mill setting, slow steady motion, no people in frame, photoreal

shots.script_line: There is no fast substitute. You cannot spin up a pulp mill in six months.
shots.on_screen: CARD over darkened mill still: 'New pulp mill: ~$2B, 3-5 years'.

shots.script_line: So who's actually paying? You are -- three purchases from now, for a product you didn't know had a passport.
shots.on_screen: Receipt push-in; paper-goods line highlights; the Ledger's stamp closes the act.

shots.script_line: The rate is public. It sits in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule under heading 4803 -- the code for tissue-grade paper -- and it took effect on [DATE -- pending src_ustr_tariff_notice].
shots.on_screen: Screen capture of the actual HTS page, heading 4803 highlighted, slow scroll.

shots.script_line: In practice, an importer is a converter with a contract, and contracts have pass-through clauses.
shots.on_screen: SEED clip: hands flipping a contract, pen taps the pass-through clause.

tool_params.prompt: close-up of hands flipping through a printed contract on a desk, pen taps a highlighted pass-through clause line, no faces visible, natural office lighting

shots.script_line: Kimberly-Clark told its investors exactly that, in its last quarterly filing: higher input costs, recovered through pricing.
shots.on_screen: Screen capture of the 10-Q sentence, highlighter sweep.

tool_params.capture_notes: highlighter sweep over the pass-through-pricing sentence

shots.script_line: Recovered through pricing. That's the polite phrase for: you.
shots.on_screen: The Ledger stamps 'recovered through pricing -> you'.

shots.script_line: So follow one roll backwards. On the shelf it's $1.10.
shots.on_screen: H3 clip: single roll on a shelf, lights dim around it -- the episode's 'hero object' motif.

tool_params.prompt: single toilet paper roll on an empty store shelf, surrounding lights slowly dim to spotlight the roll, photoreal, static-to-slow-push camera

shots.script_line: The retailer took about 25 cents... the converter -- the company that turned a two-ton pulp bale into something with a cardboard tube -- took the biggest single cut, and it took that cut after the tariff made its main input more expensive.
shots.on_screen: Waterfall chart: $1.10 decomposing into retailer / converter / mill / tree segments, each labeled as it splits.

shots.script_line: The mill in Quebec got about 30 cents. And the tree? About a nickel.
shots.on_screen: STILL: stylized cross-section -- tree -> bale -> roll -- in house style.

tool_params.prompt: stylized infographic cross-section illustration: tree, then pulp bale, then finished paper roll, left to right, house style board

shots.script_line: Every one of those numbers moved this year. Only one of them moved because of a government.
shots.on_screen: The Ledger returns; the tariff line pulses. Act break sting.
